binders: n is universally quantified over the natural numbers, including 0.
B is universally quantified over the real numbers.
After the assumptions on B, delta is universally quantified over all functions Fin n -> Real, equivalently all real families (delta(i)) indexed by i = 0, ..., n-1.
hypotheses: For every i in Fin n, |delta(i)| <= B.
conclusions: (1 - B)^n <= product over all i in Fin n of (1 + delta(i)).
The product over all i in Fin n of (1 + delta(i)) <= (1 + B)^n.
mathematical_definitions: Fin n is the n-element index set {0, 1, ..., n-1}.
Let P denote the exact finite product P = product over i in Fin n of (1 + delta(i)).
The exponents are natural-number powers formed by repeated real multiplication.
When n = 0, the product is empty and equals 1, and both zero-exponent powers equal 1.
There are no existentially quantified witnesses and no vector norm; the only size condition is the coordinatewise scalar absolute-value bound.
translation.proposition_plain_english: For every natural number n and every real number B with 0 <= B <= 1, every n-indexed real family delta satisfying |delta(i)| <= B for every index i obeys the two-sided bound (1 - B)^n <= product over i = 0 to n - 1 of (1 + delta(i)) <= (1 + B)^n.

restrictions_and_vacuity_risks: The result applies under the explicit restriction 0 <= B <= 1.
The perturbation restriction is coordinatewise: each delta(i) lies in [-B, B]. No aggregate, Euclidean, or other vector norm is present.
Because B <= 1, each factor 1 + delta(i) is nonnegative, but strict positivity is not guaranteed; when B = 1, a component delta(i) = -1 can make a factor zero.
The case n = 0 is included. The componentwise hypothesis is then vacuous, the product is empty, and both conclusions reduce to 1 <= 1.

As a chain of implications, an instance with B outside [0, 1], or a delta that violates its componentwise bound, satisfies the corresponding implication vacuously because its hypotheses are unavailable.

The proposition gives only the displayed endpoint product bounds. It does not assert strict inequalities, equality characterizations, probabilistic independence, a sum bound, an approximation error estimate, or that B is the smallest possible component bound.
